claims.text: The patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, denies smoking or recreational drug use, consumes alcohol in moderation (approximately 6 units per week), and engages in regular jogging.

Family history includes no history of cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, migraines, or neurological conditions in the immediate family; the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.
Initial triage on 07/01/26 recorded blood pressure at 160/90 mmHg and heart rate at 88 bpm.
A CT head scan performed on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormalities.
Blood tests collected on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS).

Medication records conflict regarding the initial dose of nimodipine: one record states 60 mg orally every 4 hours was started on 07/01/26, while another record states 30 mg orally every 4 hours was continued on 08/01/26 without documenting the change.
On 07/01/26, blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, headache severity was 7/10, and laboratory results showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
Potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily was prescribed on 07/01/26 to correct hypokalemia.
The patient's GP was contacted on 07/01/26 to provide an update on admission and preliminary diagnosis.
On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 08/01/26, the plan included continuing nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, repeating MRA in 48 hours, and continuing potassium chloride 1 g twice daily.
On 08/01/26, the patient received educational materials on RCVS, including advice to avoid triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, headache severity reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L).
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 10/01/26, headache severity reduced to 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted from previous tests.
On 10/01/26, the plan included maintaining nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continuing dietary measures for hyponatremia, and repeating MRA on 11/01/26.
On 10/01/26, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs.
On 11/01/26, headache severity remained at 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and the plan included continuing nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and performing a repeat MRA.
On 11/01/26, the repeat MRA showed significant improvement and resolution of cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted.

Medication records conflict regarding discharge medication: one record states nimodipine 30 mg PO QDS to be tapered over 2 weeks, while another record states amlodipine 5 mg OD was discussed with the GP.
The patient was discharged on 12/01/26 with plans for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks and advice to avoid known triggers.
